name: Wall Sit
tierNote: Not in content.md appendix B tier A or B lists, so tier C. census.json difficulty tier 2.
archetypeNote: The back rests on a wall; no GA contact archetype names a wall, so it is drawn as equipment (census: wall composer).
parentNote: content.md appendix A: bodyweight_squat parents wall_sit. Same hand archetype (none) and primary contact (standing-feet).

inherit.field: posture[1] (knees over the second toe, ankles not rolling)
inherit.why: true for this child because the wall sit holds a squat position on the same feet; knee-over-foot alignment is the standing-feet rule, and Physitrack's wall sit form adds toes slightly out with knees over the ankles (w4).
true for this child because the NHS triggers are about the knee itself, not the exercise, and the wall sit loads the same knee (w8).

claims.text: The wall sit is a simple isometric leg exercise that builds strength in a chosen squat position.

quotes.text: The wall sit is a simple isometric leg exercise for building strength in a specific squat position, or to minimize strength loss during injuries that prevent squatting and similar.

claims.text: Back to the wall, feet out in front as far as the position needs; most often hips and knees at 90 degrees.

quotes.text: Stand with your back to a wall and feet in front of it as far as needed for the desired squat position. Most commonly wall sits are done with 90-degree angles at the hip and knee, but other angles and depths can be used to work on specific positions.

claims.text: Slide down the wall into the position and hold, usually 30-60 seconds.

quotes.text: With your back supported against the wall, slide down into the chosen squat position and hold for the prescribed time, usually 30-60 seconds.

claims.text: Back flat on the wall, feet shoulder width, toes slightly out, knees directly above the ankles.

quotes.text: Keep your back flat against the wall, your feet shoulder-width apart and your toes pointed slightly outward. Make sure your knees are directly above your ankles and hold the position for as long as you can.

claims.text: Back and buttocks stay in contact with the wall.

quotes.text: Ensure your back and buttocks remain in contact with the wall.

claims.text: Programme 2-5 sets of 30-60 second holds; once 60 seconds is comfortable, make it harder (one foot lifted, single leg, or weight on the thighs).

quotes.text: The wall sit can be done for 2-5 sets of 30-60-second holds. If the athlete is able to hold for 60 seconds comfortably, variations to increase difficulty can be introduced, such as lifting one foot at a time, single-leg holds, or holding weight on the thighs.

claims.text: Heart rate and blood pressure rise as the knee bends further (tested 135 to 90 degrees, n=23), so the depth sets how hard the hold is.

quotes.text: The heart rate and blood pressure parameters produced significant inverse relationships with joint angle (r at least -0.80; P < 0.05), demonstrating that wall squat intensity can be adjusted by manipulating knee joint angle.

claims.text: In dynamic bodyweight wall and ball squats (n=16), a short heel-to-wall distance moved the knees past the toes and raised kneecap force and stress at 90-100 degrees on the way up; a 12RM wall squat study found the same at 90 degrees. Applied to the static hold by inference.

quotes.text: Sixteen participants performed a dynamic ball squat and wall squat with long HTWD and short HTWD.
patellofemoral joint force and stress were greater with a short HTWD than a long HTWD at 100° ( P = 0.007) and 90° ( P = 0.008) knee angles during squat ascent
squatting with short HTWD produced anterior knee displacement beyond the toes at higher knee angles, resulting in greater patellofemoral force and stress compared with squatting with long HTWD.
Patellofemoral force and stress were significantly greater at 90 degrees knee angle in the wall squat short compared with wall squat long

claims.text: Kneecap-joint load in wall squats is higher between 60 and 90 degrees of knee bend than between 0 and 50, so a shallower position loads the kneecap less (dynamic 12RM wall squats).

quotes.text: When the goal is to minimize patellofemoral compressive force and stress, it may be prudent to use a smaller knee angle range between 0 degrees and 50 degrees compared with a larger knee angle range between 60 degrees and 90 degrees

claims.text: Holding the breath during an isometric effort raises blood pressure further than breathing through it (handgrip study, applied here by inference).

quotes.text: These results indicate that during isometric exercise, a breath-hold enhances an exercise-induced increase in MAP

claims.text: One coach page names the quadriceps, glutes, hamstrings and calves as the muscles the wall sit works, without ranking them.

quotes.text: The wall sit primarily works the quadriceps, glutes, hamstrings, and calves.

claims.text: NHS knee pain: get advice from 111 if the knee is very painful, or locks, gives way or painfully clicks.

quotes.text: your knee locks, gives way or painfully clicks – painless clicking is normal

plate.viewWhy: Hip and knee angles (w2), knees over ankles (w4) and heel-to-wall distance (w8) read only from the side.
plate.frames: Hold convention (architecture section 1): entry pose (standing, back on the wall) then the held pose.
plate.equipment: Wall behind the lifter; floor line.
plate.start: Entry: standing with back and buttocks on the wall, feet out in front (w2, w5).
plate.end: Held pose: slid down to hips and knees at about 90 degrees (w2), knees directly above the ankles (w4), back flat on the wall (w4).

checkpoints.label: Back on wall
checkpoints.what: Back and buttocks stay on the wall.

checkpoints.label: Knees over ankles
checkpoints.what: Shins vertical, knees directly above the ankles.

checkpoints.label: 90 degrees
checkpoints.what: Hips and knees at about 90 degrees; shallower is easier.

mistake.what: Feet too close to the wall, knees pushed forward past the toes.
mistake.why: Measured in dynamic wall squats and applied to the hold: a short heel-to-wall distance moved the knees past the toes and raised kneecap-joint force and stress (w8); the form sources ask for knees over the ankles (w4).
mistake.rankNote: No source ranks wall sit faults. This is the one fault with measured consequences, and it reads from the side.

tempo.text: Set / Hold 30-60 s / Rest; 2-5 sets. Rest length is not sourced.

grip.note: Hand archetype none; no source gives a hand position.

setup.step: Back to the wall, feet out in front, shoulder width, toes slightly out.
Slide down until hips and knees are about 90 degrees.
Check the knees are right above the ankles; move the feet if not.

posture.point: Back and buttocks on the wall.

handlingMistakes.mistake: Feet too close to the wall.
handlingMistakes.fix: Walk the feet out until the knees are over the ankles.

handlingMistakes.mistake: Holding the breath through the hold.

handlingMistakes.fix: Hold higher on the wall, with less knee bend.

rows.means: The quads are doing the hold.

rows.where: Front of the knee, around the kneecap
rows.means: Feet too close to the wall, or the hold is too deep.

rows.where: Very painful knee, or the knee locks or gives way

risks.risk: Blood pressure rises during the hold, more the deeper you go.
Holding the breath raises blood pressure further during the hold.
Feet too close to the wall load the kneecap more.

zooms.right: Shin vertical, knee directly above the ankle.
zooms.wrong: Feet close to the wall, knee past the toes.

zooms.right: Back and buttocks flat on the wall.

libraryDiff.why: Library: quads primary, no secondary. Physitrack names quads, glutes, hamstrings and calves without ranking them (w11), but it is a coach page with no data. No EMG source for the wall sit was read, so the secondaries are not added.

loadProgression.text: Build to 60 seconds, then lift one foot, go single-leg, or rest weight on the thighs; depth also sets intensity.

breathing.text: Breathe steadily; holding the breath raises blood pressure further during isometric work.

anchorNote: Catalyst Athletics wall sit page read in full; Physitrack wall sit page also read in full.
